blocks.text: When ogi ferments and turns sour, when palm wine bubbles in the calabash, and when your calf muscles burn near the end of a 400-metre race, the same thing is happening: cells are releasing energy from sugar without enough oxygen.

blocks.markdown:
## Respiration releases energy

Respiration is the enzyme-controlled breakdown of food, usually glucose, inside living cells to release energy. The energy is trapped in a chemical called **ATP** (adenosine triphosphate), which the cell can spend on muscle contraction, active transport, cell division and building new molecules.

Every living cell respires all the time. There are two versions of the process, distinguished by whether oxygen is used.

### Aerobic respiration

Glucose is broken down completely, using oxygen, in the mitochondria.

glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy

blocks.caption: Aerobic respiration — the reverse, in summary form, of photosynthesis

blocks.markdown:
### Anaerobic respiration

Without oxygen, glucose is broken down only partially, so most of its energy remains locked in the products.

**In yeast and many microorganisms (alcoholic fermentation):**

glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide + energy (about 118 kJ per mole)

**In animal muscle (lactic fermentation):**

glucose → lactic acid + energy (about 150 kJ per mole)

Notice that no carbon dioxide is produced in muscle, only lactic acid. This is a favourite examination discriminator.

blocks.title: Oxygen debt
blocks.text: The volume of oxygen a person needs after strenuous exercise in order to oxidise the lactic acid that accumulated in the muscles. It explains why an athlete keeps panting hard for several minutes after crossing the finish line.

blocks.title: Why a sprinter pants after the race
blocks.prompt: Explain, step by step, why a runner's legs ache during a hard 400-metre sprint and why she continues to breathe deeply for minutes after stopping.

steps.text: During the sprint the leg muscles contract rapidly and need energy far faster than usual.
The heart and lungs cannot deliver oxygen quickly enough to supply all that energy aerobically, so the muscles supplement it with anaerobic respiration.

Anaerobic respiration in muscle converts glucose to lactic acid. Because the breakdown is incomplete, each glucose molecule yields little energy, so a great deal of glucose is used and a great deal of lactic acid builds up.
Accumulated lactic acid lowers the pH in the muscle, interfering with enzyme action and causing the burning ache and eventual muscle fatigue.
After the race, oxygen is needed to oxidise the lactic acid to carbon dioxide and water, or to convert it back to glucose in the liver. This required oxygen is the oxygen debt.
She therefore keeps breathing deeply and her heart keeps beating fast until the debt is repaid, after which breathing returns to normal and the ache subsides.

blocks.answer: The ache is caused by lactic acid from anaerobic respiration when oxygen supply cannot match demand. The continued deep breathing supplies the oxygen debt needed to remove that lactic acid.

items: Bread rises because yeast respires anaerobically and the carbon dioxide it releases forms bubbles in the dough; the ethanol evaporates during baking.
Palm wine, burukutu and beer are made by yeast fermenting sugars to ethanol.
Ogi, yoghurt and fermented cassava for fufu depend on bacteria producing lactic acid, which also preserves the food by lowering the pH.
Sewage treatment and biogas production use anaerobic bacteria to break down organic waste.

blocks.caption: Respiration is not burning, even though both use oxygen and release carbon dioxide

blocks.title: The two anaerobic equations are different
blocks.text: Write ethanol and carbon dioxide for yeast, and lactic acid only for muscle. Candidates who give carbon dioxide as a product of anaerobic respiration in muscle lose the mark every time.

points: Respiration releases energy from food inside cells and stores it as ATP.
Aerobic respiration uses oxygen, occurs in the mitochondria, breaks glucose down completely to carbon dioxide and water, and releases about 2900 kJ per mole.
Anaerobic respiration needs no oxygen, occurs in the cytoplasm and releases far less energy because the breakdown is incomplete.
Yeast produces ethanol and carbon dioxide; muscle produces lactic acid only.
Lactic acid causes muscle fatigue and creates an oxygen debt that is repaid by continued deep breathing after exercise.
